title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: For every $n$-vertex simple graph $G$, the expected number of faces when selecting an orientable embedding of $G$ uniformly at random is $O(n)$.
context_text: An embedding means a $2$-cell embedding in some orientable surface, up to orientation-preserving homeomorphism fixing the graph; such embeddings of $G$ correspond bijectively to local rotations, i.e. a choice for each vertex $v$ of a cyclic permutation of the half-edges at $v$. A uniformly random embedding thus chooses independently a uniformly random rotation at every vertex; by Euler's formula, the expected number of faces determines the average genus. Stahl proved that the expected number of faces in a random embedding of any $n$-vertex graph is at most $n\log n$ (natural logarithm). The authors show that the dipole with $n$ parallel edges has exactly $H_{n-1}+\lceil n/2\rceil^{-1}$ expected faces ($H_{n-1}$ the harmonic sum), that every multistar (a loopless multigraph with a vertex incident with all edges) with $n$ nonleaf edges is within $2/(n+1)$ of this, and deduce that adding a new vertex of degree $d$ to an embedded graph creates at most $\log(d)+1$ new faces in expectation; hence $d$-regular, and more generally $d$-degenerate, $n$-vertex graphs have at most $n\log(d)$ expected faces. They also construct graph families with linearly many expected faces but found no family with superlinearly many, which led to this conjecture. For multigraphs with maximum edge-multiplicity $\mu$ they conjecture the bound $O(n\log(2\mu))$.

title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: For every $n$-vertex multigraph $G$ with maximum edge-multiplicity $\mu$, the expected number of faces when selecting an orientable embedding of $G$ uniformly at random is $O(n\log(2\mu))$.
context_text: Conjecture 1 must be adjusted when multiple edges are allowed. The dipole family shows Conjecture 2 is tight, and a long path in which every second edge is replaced by a dipole with $\mu \geq 2$ edges gives a tight family in which each of $n$ and $\mu$ can independently tend to infinity.
